conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ve reviewed your chart and the reason you came in. You had severe abdominal pain starting early yesterday morning, is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it woke me up at 3 AM. It was like 20 out of 10—way worse than my usual pain. Left side and upper belly. I tried a little food, but it made me nauseous and I couldn’t keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you’ve had these partial bowel obstructions before, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, three times this year already. I’ve had so many surgeries—bowel resections, adhesions cut, the whole thing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an abdominal CT this afternoon. It shows a partial small bowel obstruction again, likely from adhesions. But the good news is, contrast made it into your colon, so it’s not a complete blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. So no surgery this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. We’re going to treat this conservatively—keep you NPO, give IV fluids, and let your gastric tube vent to decompress your stomach. We’ll monitor your pain and bowel function closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been off TPN for months now and gaining weight—up to 176. I was doing so well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. We’ll work to get you back to eating normally. For now, rest and decompression are key.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling? Any change in pain or nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still nauseous. The tube helps a little, but I feel bloated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable—no signs of infection or dehydration. We’re giving potassium and magnesium as needed. We’ve started hydromorphone for pain through a PCA pump so you can control it safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had bad reactions to some pain meds before. I’m allergic to a lot—fentanyl, oxycontin, meperidine…

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve noted your allergies. Hydromorphone is different, and we’re monitoring you closely. If it causes issues, we’ll adjust.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your abdominal X-ray yesterday showed some improvement in distention. Still, we’re seeing a lot of fluid output from your G-tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel foggy today. And my speech is worse—I keep stumbling over words.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I noticed that. You’ve had aphasia before, right? We’re going to consult neurology to make sure this isn’t something new.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It comes and goes. Sometimes when I’m distracted, it gets better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi. The neurology team saw you. They think your aphasia and drowsiness are likely related to your chronic condition and possibly the pain meds, not a new stroke.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They don’t think so. Your CT head was clear—no bleeding or new stroke. But we’re switching your pain med from hydromorphone to morphine because the PCA may have worsened your nausea and mental fog.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I’ve been so tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Another X-ray this morning shows your large bowel is more dilated. We’re concerned about ileus—slowed bowel function—possibly from the narcotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the pain meds are making my gut slower?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ve stopped the PCA and are giving morphine only as needed. We’ll keep you NPO a bit longer and encourage walking to stimulate your bowels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you passed gas last night, and your G-tube output has decreased.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a little better. Can I try some food?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with ice chips and see how you do. If no nausea, we’ll advance to clear liquids tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You tolerated the clear liquids well. We’re going to try a soft diet today—applesauce, broth, mashed potatoes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. And my speech is clearer today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and you’re more alert. We’re also capping your G-tube intermittently to see if you can manage without constant venting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had a small bowel movement this morning—that’s a great sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still get nauseous if the tube’s capped too long.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: But it resolves after a few hours once you uncapped it. That’s expected. Your gut is still recovering.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did another CT head and abdominal X-ray today. The head scan was normal—no new issues. The abdominal film shows the obstruction is slightly improved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: There was something about a metal object in the report?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. It’s the clip from your G-tube. It detached and is now floating in your bowel. It’s been seen before on old scans and has moved down. It’s not causing a blockage, so we’re just monitoring it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Shouldn’t it come out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It likely will pass on its own. We’ll watch for any symptoms, but no intervention is needed now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been on a regular diet since yesterday and doing well. No vomiting, pain is at your baseline, and you’re walking regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. I miss my routine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge tomorrow. We’ll make sure you’re stable on oral meds and your enoxaparin is set for home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Last night’s vitals were stable—heart rate 112, oxygen 90% on room air. A bit low on oxygen, but you’re not short of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve always had a fast heart rate—usually in the 120s. And I’ve had asthma, but it’s mild.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your history notes chronic tachycardia and asthma. As long as you’re not struggling to breathe, we’re okay to proceed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve scheduled your follow-up with surgery in two weeks. You’ll keep taking all your home meds, including gabapentin, lamotrigine, and rabeprazole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the enoxaparin for my blood thinning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue that daily. You’ve had DVTs before, so it’s important to prevent clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—your discharge instructions say to eat soft foods for a few weeks and drink plenty of fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And walk a lot to keep my bowels moving?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And call if you develop fever, severe pain, vomiting, or can’t eat or drink.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re finalizing your discharge papers. You’re doing well—eating regular food, pain controlled, and moving independently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad this episode didn’t set me back too much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. Just take it slow at home and follow up as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your final vitals are stable. We’ll discharge you this afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will review your meds and home care. Remember—soft diet, walk daily, and monitor for warning signs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And keep my G-tube capped unless I’m nauseous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and uncapping it should help symptoms. If nausea persists, call your surgeon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Discharge orders are in. You’ll go home with visiting nurse services to check in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s reassuring. I’ll follow up with my doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check—your pain is manageable, you’re alert, and you’ve had normal bowel movements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, back to my usual baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll see you in clinic, but call sooner if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your ride is here. Take care, and keep up the good work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate everything.
